title: Ambarisha's fast
hookLine: a king's Ekadashi, an angry sage and Vishnu's disc; the twice-monthly day for Vishnu
carry: ekadashi is a day given to vishnu

lines: A YEAR OF FASTS FOR VISHNU.
AN ANGRY SAGE AT THE DOOR.
cards: King Ambarisha loves Vishnu, and for a whole year he keeps the fast of the eleventh day. On the morning after the last one, it's time to break it.
Then the sage Durvasa arrives, well-known across the worlds for his temper. Ambarisha bows and invites him to eat first. Durvasa goes to bathe in the river, and takes his time.
The moment for breaking the fast is slipping away. Eat before a guest, and he insults a sage. Miss the moment, and the vow is broken.

teach.h: A SIP OF WATER. A FURIOUS SAGE.
teach.b: His priests advise a sip of water: it breaks the fast, and it isn't eating ahead of a guest. Durvasa comes back, sees it, and in a rage hurls a fiery demon at the king. Ambarisha doesn't move.
And Vishnu's spinning disc, the Sudarshana, burns the demon up and chases Durvasa across the worlds. Durvasa runs to Vishnu himself, who says: I am in the hands of my devotees. Go and ask him.
That's the Bhagavata Purana. Here's the teaching. Ekadashi isn't a diet day.
It's a day given to Vishnu, kept with love.

Ekadashi means the eleventh: eka is one, dasha is ten. The Hindu calendar follows the moon. Each lunar month has a bright half, as the moon grows, and a dark half, as it shrinks, fifteen lunar days each.

The eleventh day of each half is Ekadashi. So it comes about twice a month, on a different date on your wall calendar every time; that's why so many grandmothers keep a paper calendar with the days circled.

teach.h: FRUIT AND MILK, OR A FULL FAST.
teach.b: Those who keep it often skip grains and beans and eat fruit, milk or nuts. Some fast fully. A few keep one Ekadashi a year without even water.
The day goes to prayer, singing Vishnu's names, reading. And the fast is broken the next morning, often at a set time, just as Ambarisha tried to. A one-off vow depends on remembering.

teach.h: EKADASHI IS A DAY GIVEN TO VISHNU.
teach.b: Ekadashi comes round with the moon, and twice a month it turns a whole household back toward Vishnu.

how: Many Hindus, especially devotees of Vishnu and Krishna, observe Ekadashi, the eleventh lunar day of each fortnight, by avoiding grains and beans or fasting, spending extra time in prayer or singing Vishnu's names, and breaking the fast the next morning; the story of King Ambarisha is often told on the day.

games.q: a friend sees Ekadashi circled on your family calendar and says, 'so it's basically a cleanse day?' what fits the teaching?
o: yes: a health cleanse, twice a month.
it's a day given to Vishnu, kept with the moon.
it's a day to eat only rice.
games.why: Ekadashi is devotion first: a day for Vishnu, twice a month. Ambarisha's love, not his hunger, is what the story honors.

practice: Think back to the last time you noticed the moon: a thin sliver, half, nearly full? If you don't remember, that's fine. If you pray, say one of Vishnu's names, Hari or Narayana, slowly, three times.
If you don't, look for the moon tonight, and notice how far it is toward full or new. No fasting needed.

wordCard.voice: Ekadashi. The eleventh day of each half of the lunar month: twice a month, a fast day given to Vishnu. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit ekādaśī: the eleventh, the eleventh lunar day of each fortnight.

carryVoice: Your line: Ekadashi is a day given to Vishnu. Ambarisha gave his, and Vishnu stood by him. That's one hundred thirty.
